summary: Backend-only verification of the new admin endpoint POST /api/admin/purge-users. Wrote /app/backend/tests/test_admin_purge_users.py (pytest, 9 tests, 5 test classes) and executed against the preview URL (https://design-decided.preview.emergentagent.com). All 9 tests passed in 4.62s. Every acceptance criterion from the review request is satisfied: (1) empty body with admin session returns dry_run=true, exactly the 11 default patterns, matched_users=0 on the already-clean preview DB, sample_emails=[]; (2) custom pattern '^example-nonexistent-' correctly filters to matched_users=0; (3) no cookie -> HTTP 404 with {"detail":"Not found"}; (4) guest session (via /auth/guest) -> HTTP 404; (5) non-admin real OTP-verified user -> HTTP 404 (bonus check, tightens the auth boundary); (6) full lifecycle -- OTP-create throwaway 'purge-test-{run}-single@example.com', dry-run with '^purge-test-{run}-single' shows matched_users=1 with that email in sample_emails, confirm=true returns deleted.users=1 and deleted.user_sessions>=1, follow-up dry-run shows matched_users=0; (7) admin self-protection -- pattern '^support@' returns matched_users=0 and admin email is NOT in sample_emails; (8) cascade -- OTP-create 'purge-test-{run}-cascade@example.com', create 2 projects, dry-run reports cascade.projects=2, confirm delete returns deleted.projects=2 and deleted.user_sessions>=1, follow-up dry-run 0; (9) GET on the same URL returns 405 (method not allowed, as expected). Test suite cleans up its own throwaway users via a module-scoped teardown that re-issues a scoped purge with confirm=true.
critical_code_review_comments: server.py L720: `patterns = [p.strip() ... ] or list(_DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_PATTERNS)` -- if the caller sends only whitespace/commas the fallback silently swaps in the 11 default patterns. That's a benign choice but the API contract should document it (or refuse). Consider returning 400 if the caller passed a non-empty `patterns` string that trimmed to zero regexes, so ops can't accidentally think their narrow pattern ran when the defaults did.

server.py L723: `{"$or": [{"email": {"$regex": p}} for p in patterns]}` -- Mongo regexes are unanchored + case-sensitive. Emails are stored lowercased at signup, but if a support ticket ever calls this with `Support@` (capital S), the admin-skip $nin still uses the lowercased admin email, which is correct, but the regex itself would miss capital-letter emails. Fine given how emails are normalized, but worth an explicit note or a `re.IGNORECASE` option.

server.py L720-726: no server-side sanity cap on the number of regex patterns or their compile cost. `max_length=2000` on the input string is fine, but a malicious/panicked admin could paste a catastrophic-backtracking regex (`(a+)+$`) that stalls Mongo. Consider server-side compiling each pattern with `re.compile` + a timeout / length check per pattern (e.g. reject patterns >200 chars or with nested quantifiers).

server.py L728: `.to_list(length=10000)` -- silent truncation. If a real production purge ever exceeded 10k matches the cascade counts would be under-reported and the subsequent `delete_many(regex_filter)` would still delete everything, which would then reconcile the counts -- but the returned `matched_users` and `sample_emails` would understate reality. Consider paginating or at least logging when the cap is hit.

server.py L766-769: `db.sessions.update_many` (note: `sessions`, not `user_sessions`) pulls victim user_ids from a `user_ids` array field. This is a different collection from `user_sessions`. If this collection isn't actually used elsewhere it's harmless, but it's easy to confuse with `user_sessions` on a future read of the code. Add a one-line comment naming which feature owns `sessions.user_ids` (looks like it's the multi-user collaboration/share-session table).

server.py L770: `users_del = await db.users.delete_many(regex_filter)` -- this reuses the compound `regex_filter` that already contains the `$nin admin_emails` guard, which is exactly right; keep this invariant in mind if anyone refactors the filter construction into separate variables.
test_credentials: Admin: support@use-bracket.com / Bracket@123 via POST /api/auth/login. Non-admin real users are minted per-test via OTP_TEST_MODE=1 dev_code flow with random emails prefixed 'purge-test-{run_id}-'.
seed_data_creation: Two throwaway OTP-verified users per test run ('purge-test-{run_id}-single@example.com' and 'purge-test-{run_id}-cascade@example.com') plus 2 projects on the cascade user. All are deleted by the tests themselves (each ends with confirm=true purge) AND by a module-scoped autouse teardown that re-purges '^purge-test-{run_id}-'. Verified post-run: sample_emails for the run-scoped pattern returns []. One non-admin user ('purge-test-{run_id}-nonadmin@example.com') from TestAuthBoundary is also cleaned up by the same teardown.
context_for_next_testing_agent: The purge endpoint is at POST /api/admin/purge-users. It's registered under the `api` router (prefix /api) and gated by `auth_current_admin` which returns HTTP 404 (not 401/403) on any auth failure -- that's deliberate to hide the endpoint's existence. To exercise it, log in as support@use-bracket.com / Bracket@123 via POST /api/auth/login (session cookie name is 'session_token', httpOnly). Body schema: {"patterns": "comma,separated,regex", "confirm": bool} -- both optional; empty patterns falls back to 11 built-in automation prefixes (see _DEFAULT_AUTOMATION_PATTERNS in server.py). Always call with confirm=false first for a dry-run and to preview `sample_emails`. When creating test users to purge, use OTP_TEST_MODE=1 flow: POST /api/auth/otp/request returns {dev_code} in preview -- verify with POST /api/auth/otp/verify. The endpoint hard-excludes admin emails from the regex filter via a $nin guard, so pattern '^support@' returns matched_users=0. All 11 default patterns match zero users on the current preview DB -- ops has already cleaned it.
rca_of_the_issue: N/A -- new-feature verification. No bugs found. Endpoint behaves exactly per spec: correct 404 for unauth/guest/non-admin, correct dry-run defaults, correct cascade counts, correct admin self-protection, correct delete-then-recount-to-0 lifecycle.
